svg.title: What TSA's pages say about locking a checked bag: an unlocked bag, TSA recognized locks, other locks that may be cut, TSA's stated position on the locks, inspection notices and claims.
svg.text: TSA locks and checked bags
What TSA's pages say
If the bag is not locked
Most checked bags are screened without
a physical search. If an item alarms,
TSA says an officer will simply open
and screen the bag.
TSA recognized locks
TSA has universal master keys under
agreements with Safe Skies Luggage Locks
and Travel Sentry, so certain branded
locks may not have to be cut. The
packaging should say TSA may open it.
Other locks
If TSA cannot open a locked bag through
other means, the lock may have to be cut.
TSA says it is not liable for damage to
locked bags opened for security purposes.
Soft-sided bags: zippers are not damaged.
TSA's stated position
TSA has no position on whether these
locks work as a security measure, and
says it will remove them if necessary
during an inspection.
If something is lost or damaged
A notice of baggage inspection goes in a
bag that was physically inspected.
During screening: file a claim with TSA.
On the way to the plane or baggage
claim: contact the airline.
The claims page
Letter in 4 to 6 weeks; up to 6 months to
investigate. Many claims are denied when
officers did not open the bag. The three
pages show no update dates.
Sources: three TSA pages; read Nov. 13, 2026
